summary: FireTwin is a fire-safety digital twin of an ISS lab module, built on NASA microgravity combustion data. In microgravity, flames depend entirely on airflow for oxygen and smoke drifts instead of rising, so fire-safety intuition from Earth doesn’t carry over to space. You set the cabin conditions (material, oxygen, airflow and pressure) and ignite a fire in a 3D module. FireTwin predicts whether the fire keeps burning, which smoke detector trips and when, and which suppression action works best, then applies that action and predicts again. Every prediction comes from a model trained on 349 NASA tests from BASS-II, FLEX, Saffire-I and Saffire-II. Each one shows a trust level and links back to the most similar tests. Inputs outside the tested range are flagged. An AI assistant explains the results and answers questions from NASA reports with citations, but it never produces the numbers: all of them come from the model, and any AI answer with an unsupported figure is thrown out.
details:
What it does and how it works
FireTwin is a fire-safety digital twin of an ISS lab module, built on NASA microgravity combustion data. Users set the cabin conditions (material, oxygen, airflow, pressure) and ignite a fire inside an interactive 3D model of the spacecraft. FireTwin predicts whether the fire keeps burning, which smoke detector trips and when, and which suppression action works best. It then applies that action and predicts again, so users see the full emergency play out. Every prediction comes from models trained on 349 NASA tests from BASS-II, FLEX, Saffire-I and Saffire-II, with a trust level and links to the tests behind it.

System architecture and design
FireTwin is built in layers, each with one job. A data pipeline turns raw NASA PSI tables into a clean, labelled dataset, and every label traces back to its source table cell. A training stage builds per-fuel logistic regression models with physics-based features, such as the U-shaped airflow boundary where flames die from oxygen starvation at low airflow and blow-off at high airflow. A model is used only if it beats a baseline in cross-validation. On top of that sit dedicated services for prediction, smoke detection, suppression planning, retrieval over NASA reports, and PDF reporting. Thin FastAPI routes expose them to a React front end.

Our core principle is that tools compute and the LLM only writes words. All numbers come from deterministic Python. Gemini writes explanations and answers questions with citations, and a grounding layer throws out any answer containing a number or test ID it can’t trace to its input. A multi-agent pipeline (Analyst, Strategist, Safety Critic, Report Writer) drafts and reviews suppression plans, with approval coming from rule checks, never the LLM. If the AI is unavailable, the whole system falls back to the deterministic pipeline and keeps running offline.

Benefits and impact
FireTwin turns years of NASA microgravity combustion research into a decision tool that anyone can use to explore spacecraft fire scenarios safely, without running experiments in orbit. In space, flames feed only on airflow and smoke drifts instead of rising, so intuition from Earth fails. FireTwin makes that behavior visible and actionable, supporting crew training, mission planning and safer habitat design as missions get longer and commercial stations come online.

Tech stack
Python, FastAPI, Gemini, Chroma (RAG), React, TypeScript, Vite, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Docker, and NASA PSI data.

Creativity
FireTwin combines a 3D model of the spacecraft with a data-driven combustion model: users watch the fire and smoke move through the module while the model makes every call behind the scenes. Suppression actions are evaluated by re-running the model on the changed conditions, so recommendations come from NASA data rather than a fixed rulebook. Our grounded AI design means users get natural-language explanations they can trust.

Factors considered
We prioritized trust and transparency. Labels inferred from gas sensors and filled-in values are clearly marked, and actions with no NASA test data (water mist, cut power) are ranked last instead of guessed. Recommendations call out safety trade-offs; for example, turning the fans off starves the flame but also stops smoke from reaching the detectors.
